assessments.reason: Automerge documents are histories of changes over structured (map/list/text) data, a plausible fit for structured collaborative documents; ID arrays/triples and generic federation are not equivalent data models, which bounds but does not negate the fit.
Merge rules are deterministic per type and all nodes agree on the chosen value, so any two documents can always be merged and replicas converge; concurrent conflicts remain inspectable.

No measured workload or scale case exists for this design's workloads; full-history storage has real overhead and nothing in the evidence quantifies it. Adoption now would be an unmeasured commitment.

Actor identifiers do not establish authenticated signer identity; signed envelopes must remain an independent layer. Adopting now as the shared layer does not by itself satisfy signed-history compatibility.

The sync protocol is transport-agnostic and per document, the storage format is a compact binary format, and a first-party Rust API documents the sync surface; the concepts documentation is JavaScript-focused, which is a caveat, not a blocker.
Automerge carries no authority model; the design's authority boundary would still have to be built and enforced outside it, so adoption now leaves this criterion unmet by the adopted component.
An isolated adapter scopes Automerge to the structured-document workloads where its history-of-changes model fits, and keeps non-equivalent models (ID arrays/triples, generic federation) outside it.
The adapter inherits the same deterministic merge rules and convergence guarantee, applied only inside the adapter's document boundary.
Still unmeasured today; this option is defined by running the representative workload benchmark before any adoption, so the criterion is answered by the revisit gate rather than asserted now.
The adapter keeps signed envelopes as an independent layer by construction, and the revisit conditions include signed-origin interoperability tests before adoption.
The per-document, transport-agnostic sync protocol is exactly the seam an adapter needs, and the Rust sync API is first-party.
Authority stays in the existing layer; the adapter is a data-plane component behind that boundary and grants nothing on its own.
Adopting none provides no history-of-changes structured-document capability; if that workload materializes, the criterion is simply unmet.
Adopting none adds no deterministic convergence machinery; concurrent-change handling stays whatever the current design already has.
Adopting none avoids the unmeasured history/merge overhead entirely; the B10 disposition records adopt-none as the valid result if measurements do not justify that overhead.
The existing signed-envelope layer is untouched, so nothing in this option puts signed-history compatibility at risk.
Adopting none gains no CRDT interoperability; cross-language document exchange would need another mechanism if it becomes a requirement.
The authority boundary is unchanged by adopting none; no new component is introduced inside it.

criteria.question: Does the option fit the data model and history the design needs (structured documents with inspectable change history)?
Does the option provide deterministic convergence for concurrent changes?
Is the option's scale/performance cost (memory, CPU, wire) established for representative workloads?
Is the option compatible with signed history (authenticated signer identity stays verifiable)?
Does the option interoperate across languages and formats (including the Rust core and the per-document sync protocol)?
Does the option preserve the design's authority boundary (actor identity is not authority; grants stay in the existing layer)?

decision.reason: Adopt-now is rejected: no measured workload/scale case exists, and signatures/authority remain external to Automerge. The conditional candidate is an isolated adapter after V2 conflict reports and the representative workload benchmark (memory/CPU/wire plus signed-origin interoperability tests); adopt-none remains the valid final result if those measurements do not justify the history/merge overhead. This preserves the conflict-report-first posture and the contingent-tier trigger recorded on #9143 / S1.41.

experiments.method: Benchmark Automerge on a representative structured-document workload (memory, CPU, and wire cost of full-history documents and sync), plus signed-origin interoperability tests, per the B10 revisit conditions. Planned only in this slice; no runs were performed, so no measurements are asserted.

limitations: The validator checks structural completeness and traceability only, not factual truth; this artifact is a synthesis of the B10 source ledger (evidence checked 2026-11-12) plus a fresh primary-source re-read of the three Automerge references on 2026-11-14, which confirmed the cited claims (history-of-changes documents, deterministic merge rules, per-document sync assuming a reliable in-order stream).
No measurements were run in this slice: scale/performance is unmeasured by design (contingent tier), so every scale assessment is unknown rather than estimated.
The Automerge documentation is living and undated; behavior claims hold as documented at the 2026-11-14 access time.
No code was compiled against Automerge in this slice; cross-language findings rest on the documented Rust sync API and the JavaScript-focused concepts documentation.

options.label: Adopt Automerge now as the shared CRDT layer
Defer: isolated Automerge adapter after V2 conflict reports and a representative workload benchmark
Adopt none: keep the current design without Automerge

question: Against the shared CRDT criteria for #9143 (statement S1.41), should ID/Atlas adopt Automerge now, adopt it later through an isolated adapter, or adopt none?
